transcription.text: All right, well, welcome back everyone to the Neo Cloud Summit in SF.
My name is Steve Ho, I'm the Head of Research at Silicon Data.
And today I have the great pleasure of interviewing Angela from Cerebrus.
And honestly, and I say this genuinely, this is one of the interviews,
and I saw the list that I was most excited about.
You guys are a legendary company, you know, there is a lot written about you, right?
Some true, I'm sure some are also, you know, myth.
And I want to actually get you finding out the answers to some of those questions.
So first of all, you know, what can you just tell us quickly to those
in the audience who are somehow for whatever reason or now, what is Cerebrus?
So Cerebrus is an AI company.
We design, build and manufacture our own chips, which you can actually see here.
So this is the largest chip in the world.
It's an actual chip that's ever been productionized.
It's about 50 times larger than a GPU.
That's pretty cool.
And you're the first to bring a prop and that's one hell of a prop.
We were, thank you.
We were the first to be able to build a chip of this size,
because not only is it about the chip architecture,
it's actually also about the power and cooling.
So to be able to run a chip like this requires a huge amount of thought
into the design of dense power delivery as well as cooling,
which we did, you know, eight years ago.
And we were ahead of the industry in doing that.
A lot of folks now are working on larger reticle sizes,
bringing memory and compute closer together.
And I think we were one step ahead of the market in getting that started.
So it has become very popular to start referring to things. There's this new
thing called inference chip. Would you say it's a fair characterization
that Cerebras is an inference chip?
We actually work for inference and training.
Okay.
But the bulk of our business now is an inference,
just with the explosion of demand and how much differentiation we have
in that particular workload.
And can you just for our audience explain what is an inference chip?
Why do we need Cerebras when we already have, you know, the NVIDIA GPUs?
So first, there's two parts of an AI workload.
First is training the model.
That's the act of actually teaching the model, making it intelligent.
The second part is inference, which is the act of actually using the model.
So that's when we send a request to chat GPT and we get a response back.
So with inference, there's a lot of different points that you can optimize for.
NVIDIA GPUs were designed to be very good at running high batches,
where they can run a lot of parallel compute.
However, the high batch comes at the cost of interactivity.
Within inference, there are workloads where you need a lot of real-time user interactivity.
So for example, think of if you're trying to code with an AI agent,
you want your request to come back as quickly as possible.
One of the use cases that I use now is actually editing Excel sheets with AI,
which is basically, you know, just type in the prompt of what rows I want
or what calculations I want done and the AI will just do it.
But even waiting 30 seconds, although it doesn't sound that long, is actually a long time.
Because when I'm trying to do this live in a meeting or when I'm trying to do multiplayer
with another partner, it's always this question of should I ask the AI to do it
or should I just do it myself? Like, which one's going to be faster?
So that's why people come to Cerebrus is we actually deliver the fastest inference in the world.
The way we do that is by having a huge amount of SRAM memory and compute on the same piece of silicon.
So that allows us to have incredibly high memory bandwidth.
It's what we optimize for and inference is very memory bandwidth constraint.
So that allows us to generate much faster tokens and deliver better experienced users.
So that's a great, you know, a point and that makes a lot of sense.
So there is in the inference chip industry, there is you
and there is another legendary company called Etched, right?
I honestly don't know too much about them.
Other than the fact that I know they're very famous.
They've got a lot long list, very, you know, famous legendary backers and so.
And then, of course, beyond that, you have seen other, you know,
inference chips coming from including, I think, OpenAI itself released Jalapeno.
And, you know, I think Grok is something, you know, in that direction as well.
How do you think about this space of it?
There seems to be a notion that seems to be like we are seeing a wave of many,
many different types of inference chips that are all fast and optimized in different ways.
How do you see this eventually shake out and what differentiates Cerebrus from the crowd?
I think the reason why you see a multitude of inference chip companies now is
that workload has solidified and it's become something that's being used at production scale.
What that allows chip companies to do is actually create hardware
that's optimized for this particular workload.
So that's sort of the reason why, in addition to some of the players
that have been here for a long time, like Nvidia,
we start to see a crop of new inference chip companies.
Many of them are actually going after the same type of workload
that Cerebrus is optimized for, which is this interactive workload.
And when you design a chip specifically for inference,
you can then make the trade-offs necessary to really work
for whatever you're trying to optimize for, whether that's interactivity,
low power per token, high batch, or something else.
So I think we'll continue to see this trend of additional companies
coming to the market for inference.
I think it's actually a really good thing.
So I am an economist, rather boring.
I don't come from a tech background.
And when I look at a market that seems to have new and new products
coming into the scene that looks incredibly infragmented,
I think about economies of scale and whether or not this market
will eventually be able to accommodate so many different types of chips
that are highly customized for particular workloads.
What is your perspective on that?
Do you think the market can just keep accommodating
hundreds of different types of heterogeneous chips?
Or do you think this is just a phase
during which everyone's trying to fight
that to be one of the few that remains and captures the market?
That's a great question.
And I think what we've seen in other industries,
I used to be in the ads industry as an example,
is there's always an ebb and flow.
So when you have new optimizations in ads,
it was video ads versus text ads versus digital on-site ads.
There's always going to be new products
that are created to optimize for those different needs.
And then a few years later,
as those needs start to get more and more similar,
you see a consolidation again.
So always an ebb and flow of new products being created
and then consolidation.
I think right now we're in the phase of new products being created
within the chip industry for inference.
There's such a large demand for inference,
but there's also so many different workloads
and different points of optimization.
What I expect is in a few years, there will be consolidation.
Certainly not every company that's making a chip right now
will be successful.
But those that are able to actually reach scale
and have true differentiation will continue to survive.
And more importantly,
the companies that are able to continue innovating
are the ones that will survive.
And one thing I have noticed about Cerubris
is something I've learned myself recently
is that within similar data,
we have a thing called Silicon Mark
and we do physical benchmarking
and looking at latency of models
being served at different data centers.
And Cerubris actually comes up as one of the providers of tokens
and consistently being among the fastest,
if not always consistently the fastest.
I had even no idea that Cerubris being a chip company
was actually directly selling tokens.
And prior to our interview,
you were telling me a little bit about
how you actually directly run clouds.
So this is new to me.
And can you explain to me a little bit
what the thinking behind that is?
So we first launched inference in 2024.
And at that time, we knew we had a product
that would allow people to run completely different use cases
for inference with the speed.
The challenge is most of our customers
don't have their own data centers.
So how do we get this product into the hands of customers?
We came up with serving this through our own cloud
because we knew that if we could distribute this product
and make it really easy for customers,
including AI native and digital native customers
to actually use our inference
with very little barrier to entry,
then the product would explode.
So that was the decision we made
and why we decided to bring up our own cloud and sell direct.
And I think a secondary benefit of it
is it allowed us to be very connected with the end customer
and very connected with making their workload successful.
So rather than a traditional hardware model
of just shipping your hardware to the dock
and then it's like, "Good luck. Let us know how it goes."
We're actually responsible for the end success of the customer,
making sure they really get the speeds that we advertised,
making sure that their end users are seeing better experiences,
which typically is leading to higher revenue,
higher engagement, higher retention for our customers.
So on Twitter, X, there's recently there was this saying
that everyone is trying to become a Neo cloud.
Is it fair to say that Cerebrus is also in a way becoming a Neo cloud?
How do you think about this identity thing?
Like to get the AI, for example,
they are a manual service inference provider
that sells tokens, but then at some point,
I decided rather than paying through the nose
for a renting GPUs that would just own their own GPUs,
also sell, offer a GPU for rent.
So it seems like everyone is increasingly
taking on these multiple identities.
Do you think of Cerebrus as ultimately a chip provider
that still was product chips?
Everybody just happens to sell tokens?
Or do you think the inference is actually going to become
the main identity where selling chips to others
become more incidental?
So we actually do both.
We sell direct tokens and we also sell hardware to Neo clouds
and to others who want to use our hardware
to build their own businesses.
And I think we've actually been very successful this way.
As I mentioned, having our own cloud allows us
to have that close connection to customers,
but we don't feel a strong need to be the only way
to distribute our tokens to market.
We are very happy to,
and we welcome working with Neo clouds who can use Cerebrus
and then build their own differentiation on top of it,
whether that is software level differentiation,
pricing differentiation, distribution differentiation.
We welcome that type of partnership
because ultimately that's what makes us successful
and able to scale across not just the US,
but the entire world and make our inference accessible
to everybody.
So for us, that's the strategy, we're doing both.
I think that at large,
the reason why there's so much interest
in everyone becoming a Neo cloud
is because there's a huge demand for inference,
but the constraining factor across the industry
right now is power.
So people are treating power as actually the currency,
power and compute as the currency.
And as a Neo cloud, you actually get to own that.
And you basically have gold that you can then sell.
So I think there's kind of a recognition
that there's a lot of value in this part of the stack right now,
especially in such a power constrained world.
And I think that's why so many people are flocking
to this part of the industry.
And just to wrap up, what's coming next?
What's the lies beyond the horizon for Cerebrus
for something we should look forward to?
We recently announced that in our future generation hardware,
we will not only have the wafer scale,
it's already really unique,
but we will also be stacking memory on top of our compute.
So we're going 3D.
Wow.
And that's going to allow us to have a huge amount
of memory capacity per chip.
This is DRAN directly bonded to our wafer
at super fast memory bandwidth.
So that's the next big innovation that we have coming up.
Mind blowing is super exciting.
Well, thank you so much for joining us today and educating me.
And yeah, look forward to learning from you again in the future.
Thank you, very nice to meet you, Steve.
